To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the generalization error of knowledge graph embedding methods can be bounded in terms of a quantity that is proportional to the number of triples that are not in the training set but are present in the test set, and (b) this quantity can be bounded in a way that depends on the number of triples in the knowledge base and on the number of entities and relations.

knowledge graph completion is a hard learning problem (i.e., the generalization error bounds are large) and that knowledge graph embedding methods perform better than random guessing, but not as good as one would expect based on the generalization error bound.

(i) the missing completely at randomized model is a good model of knowledge graphs; (ii) the generalization error of knowledge graph embedding methods is bounded in terms of the empirical loss and a term that measures the distance between the true model and the missing completely at-random model; (iii) the distance between the missing completely at- random model and the true model is bounded in terms the number of missing entries in the knowledge graph.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, under the missing completely random setting, knowledge graph embedding methods perform as well as any other method that is based on a low-rank assumption of the knowledge graph tensor.
knowledge graph embedding methods do not generalize as well as they should, but they do generalize better than random.
knowledge graph embedding methods do generalize well under the missing completely random assumption.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
knowledge graph embedding methods can be viewed as a special case of the classical probabilistic latent factor model with a specific choice of prior distribution over the latent factors.
, knowledge graph completion is a special type of supervised learning, where the labels (the missing edges in the graph) can be viewed as a function of the features (the entities in the graph).
knowledge graph embedding methods can be seen as a probabilistic model for the data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the success of knowledge graph embedding is not due to some specific properties of knowledge graphs, but rather to their similarity to i.i.d. training data.
the success of knowledge graph embedding methods relies on the fact that the data is not i.i.d. (and thus classical learning theory results do not apply).

the generalization performance of knowledge graph embedding methods is not necessarily due to their ability to model the data generating distribution, but is rather due to the fact that they are able to capture a certain structure of the knowledge graph, which we call the structural distribution.
